strategy_title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
strategy_text: Investigate how autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents can be measured objectively, reproducibly, and meaningfully across diverse tasks and operating conditions. Build an evaluation framework that distinguishes superficial task completion from correctness, robustness, and dependable behavior. Audit representative agent benchmarks for task-selection effects, environmental variability, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Define operational measures for end-to-end success, partial completion, error severity, recovery, repeat-trial consistency, tool-use correctness, and resources per successful outcome. Specify how to evaluate stochastic agents, long dependency chains, long-running tasks, external tools, and changing environments. Propose repeated-trial protocols, uncertainty intervals, failure-distribution reporting, and comparisons under controlled compute, time, tool, and monetary budgets. State the evidence and replication needed for defensible reliability claims; separate benchmark-specific gains from general improvements. Deliver a protocol with task strata, outcome rubrics, baseline comparisons, statistical analysis, and explicit limits on what its results can establish.

reasoning_steps.title: Define a protocol-specific reliability target
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix a task distribution D, an execution budget, model/prompt/tool versions, an r-run execution protocol, and a correctness rubric. For a task drawn from D, let Y_j be actual binary correctness of run j, A_j the routine oracle's acceptance, and R_j the reference judge's acceptance. Define p = E[(1/r) sum_j Y_j], a random-run success rate for this protocol, and z = E[(1/r) sum_j R_j]. This target is not probability that all r runs succeed, pass-at-r, or probability of an indefinitely safe workflow.

reasoning_steps.title: Replace perfect reference correctness with explicit error allowances
reasoning_steps.argument: For a uniformly selected run within the task batch, suppose P(R=1,Y=0) <= epsilon_plus and P(R=0,Y=1) <= epsilon_minus, with both allowances in [0,1]. These are unconditional error masses on the target distribution, not conditional error rates given acceptance or failure. They permit arbitrary dependence between A, R, and Y. If false rejection is unconstrained, use epsilon_minus=1. No supplied data establish either allowance.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive sharp population identification bounds
reasoning_steps.argument: Write f_plus=P(R=1,Y=0) and f_minus=P(R=0,Y=1). Partitioning the four possible (R,Y) outcomes gives p=z-f_plus+f_minus. Consequently max(0,z-epsilon_plus) <= p <= min(1,z+epsilon_minus). The endpoints are attainable without further restrictions: for the lower endpoint, label min(epsilon_plus,z) of the R=1 mass incorrect and all R=0 mass incorrect; for the upper endpoint, label all R=1 mass correct and min(epsilon_minus,1-z) of the R=0 mass correct. These assignments also satisfy the opposite error allowance, because its error mass is zero. Thus no uniformly narrower population interval follows from z and these allowances alone, even if the joint distribution of A and R is known.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct estimators using independent task units, not independent runs
reasoning_steps.argument: On N evaluation tasks let X_i=(1/r) sum_j A_ij and q_hat=(1/N) sum_i X_i. On m audit tasks where both judges score every run, let W_k=(1/r) sum_j(R_kj-A_kj) and w_hat=(1/m) sum_k W_k. Assume the evaluation clusters are independent and identically sampled, as are the audit clusters, and both follow the same target distribution and execution protocol. Dependence within a task is unrestricted, including dependence across its runs and judges. Then X_i lies in [0,1], W_k lies in [-1,1], and E[q_hat+w_hat]=E[A]+E[R-A]=z. Independence between the evaluation and audit panels is not needed for the union-bound argument below, though each panel must satisfy its own cluster assumptions.

reasoning_steps.title: Obtain a finite-sample confidence interval
reasoning_steps.argument: For 0<alpha<1 and positive integers N,m,r, put h_N=sqrt(log(4/alpha)/(2N)), h_m=sqrt(2 log(4/alpha)/m), eta=h_N+h_m, and c=clip(q_hat+w_hat,0,1). The bounded-variable concentration inequality gives P(|q_hat-E[A]|>h_N)<=alpha/2 and P(|w_hat-E[R-A]|>h_m)<=alpha/2. Specifically, for independent variables in an interval of length b, the centered sample mean has moment-generating function at most exp(t^2 b^2/(8n)); applying exponential Markov bounds to both tails and optimizing t yields 2 exp(-2n h^2/b^2). Here b=1 and b=2 respectively. A union bound therefore gives |q_hat+w_hat-z|<=eta with probability at least 1-alpha. Projection onto [0,1] cannot increase distance to z. Combining this event with the preceding identification bounds yields L=max(0,c-eta-epsilon_plus) and U=min(1,c+eta+epsilon_minus), with P(L<=p<=U)>=1-alpha.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate statistical uncertainty from unvalidated reference assumptions
reasoning_steps.argument: The preceding coverage statement is conditional on the error allowances being valid; it does not validate them. If a separate calibration procedure supplies simultaneous valid allowances with probability at least 1-beta, the same construction covers with probability at least 1-alpha-beta by another union bound, provided calibration targets these same error masses and protocol. Independence from calibration is not required for that union bound. Unknown systematic reference error must not be replaced by zero, and agreement among similar judges does not supply beta or either allowance.

reasoning_steps.title: Show why agreement cannot identify correctness
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider observed outputs A=R=1 on every run. One possible world has Y=1 always; another has Y=0 always. The observable judge records are identical, but p is respectively 1 or 0. Mixtures realize every intermediate p. Without a justified false-certification allowance or other correctness information, reliability is therefore unidentified despite perfect agreement. With epsilon_plus=epsilon_minus=1, the derived interval correctly becomes [0,1]. This is a logical counterexample to agreement-based certification, not an observed agent result.

reasoning_steps.title: Provide an independently derived dependence control
reasoning_steps.argument: For a proposed coverage test, draw one task type T~Bernoulli(1/2) and set all five repeated outcomes A_j=R_j=Y_j=T. The target p is 1/2. If the five repeats are incorrectly treated as five independent Bernoulli trials, observing five successes gives the conventional one-sided exact-binomial lower limit (1/20)^(1/5) at alpha=1/20. This exceeds 1/2 because 1/20>1/32. Five successes occur with probability 1/2 under the actual clustered process, so that purported 95% lower bound excludes the true value with probability at least 1/2. Counting task clusters instead avoids this unsupported fivefold sample-size claim. This construction independently demonstrates the failure mode recorded in the pointer-only ledger, without claiming inspection of its original example.

reasoning_steps.title: State what the construction contributes and what it does not
reasoning_steps.argument: This is a sufficient measurement construction, not a claim that separate oracle estimation and discrepancy auditing are necessary. Directly estimating the reference acceptance rate on audited tasks, followed by the same error allowances, is also valid and may be tighter. The proposed discrepancy construction can exploit a larger routine-evaluation panel, but no universal precision advantage is established. The sharpness claim concerns population identification, not optimality of the conservative confidence interval. No engineering intervention, actual benchmark, or deployment generalization has been evaluated.

Distribution matching gives E[A]+E[R-A]=E[R]. Task averages have the stated ranges regardless of within-task dependence. Concentration needs independent clusters within each panel, but the subsequent union bound does not require independence between panels.

The two-sided bounded-variable tail bound with range lengths one and two gives alpha/2 for each stated radius. On their joint event the sum is within eta of z. Projection cannot increase distance to z in [0,1], and subtracting or adding the corresponding error allowance yields valid endpoints.

The two worlds have identical observed A,R records and different correctness. Mixing their latent correctness realizes intermediate success rates. With both allowances one, the interval endpoints reduce to zero and one.

strategy_runs.strategy_title: Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
strategy_runs.strategy_text: Map how agents fail during extended, multi-step tasks and determine which failures are detectable, recoverable, or silently corrupt later results. Examine incorrect reasoning and plans, tool misuse, incomplete observations, stale or compressed context, instruction misunderstandings, environmental changes, and accumulated state errors. Trace concrete failure chains from initiating fault through subsequent actions to user-visible consequences; distinguish model limitations from architecture, orchestration, memory, interface, and environment failures. Investigate detection of silent errors, calibrated uncertainty versus actual failure, retry and replanning policies, escalation, and safe termination. Analyze checkpointing, state reconstruction, independent verification, rollback, idempotency, and human intervention as recovery mechanisms. For each mechanism, specify assumptions, failure modes, and measurable recovery criteria; compare recovery against restarting and continuing without intervention. Develop fault-injection scenarios and trace-based analyses that reveal propagation and test whether recovery restores correct state rather than merely producing a plausible answer. Deliver a failure taxonomy, causal workflow maps, and a prioritized set of falsifiable experiments, distinguishing observed evidence from proposed mechanisms.

reasoning_steps.title: 1. Separate business effects, service records, agent state, and audit state
reasoning_steps.argument: Let o denote one intended operation, k its protocol key, and p its complete canonical payload. Define state S=(E,D,Q,A,V,J). E is the durable business-effect ledger: entries contain effect ID, key, payload, and an evaluator-only attribution to o. N_o counts actual effects attributable to o, including those created under a mistakenly regenerated key. D is the service's durable map k -> (payload, result, effect ID), not an independent correctness oracle. Q contains request and acknowledgment envelopes, each with a distinct attempt ID. A contains agent memory and its durable checkpoint, including intended k,p. V is the entire agent-accessible event history. J is evaluator-only scheduling and fault history. Initially E and D are empty for the operations tested. The benchmark uses a synthetic durable append as its business effect; treating a database row as evidence of a real shipment would require a separate oracle.

reasoning_steps.title: 2. Define transport, timeout, and crash semantics
reasoning_steps.argument: Sending creates a request envelope in Q but changes neither E nor D. A dropped envelope is permanently removed without delivery. A delayed envelope remains eligible for later delivery, including after a retry. An acknowledgment is a separate envelope and can independently be delivered, dropped, or delayed. Timeout appends a fixed timeout event to V; it does not cancel an outstanding request or imply noncommitment. A service crash preserves E and D and discards volatile work. A crash before an atomic commit leaves neither write; a crash after it leaves both. Agent restoration restores A from its checkpoint but changes neither E nor D. The scheduler must explicitly record the disposition of every outstanding envelope; a crash is not an implicit request drop.

reasoning_steps.title: 3. Specify the agent observation boundary and ambiguous pair
reasoning_steps.argument: For paired histories, use the same local intent, serialized outgoing request, checkpoint, logical timeout time, returned bytes, headers, error metadata, tool access, and visible resource counters. In H0, drop the initial request before processing; in H1, process it and drop its acknowledgment. Hide E,D,J and queue internals from the agent. At the recovery decision, the specified projection V,A is identical, while evaluator-visible N_o is respectively 0 and 1. This constructs indistinguishability inside the abstract interface; it does not establish that a real harness prevents timing, billing, memory, or tool-status leakage. Any such leakage must be audited rather than assumed away.

reasoning_steps.title: 4. Define the atomic deduplicating service
reasoning_steps.argument: Processing a request (k,p) is one serialized transaction. If k is absent, append exactly one effect e to E and set D[k]=(p,result(e),e) atomically and durably, then enqueue an acknowledgment. If k is present with the same complete payload, enqueue its saved result without changing E or D. If k is present with a different payload, return a conflict without an effect. Retries retain k,p; distinct intended operations have distinct keys. There is no record eviction during any request's possible arrival horizon. No other actor changes E or D. The effect must actually be within this atomic boundary: atomically recording an intention before calling a nontransactional external API does not satisfy the premise.

reasoning_steps.title: 5. Prove the safety invariant
reasoning_steps.argument: For every key k, let n_k be its effect count. The invariant is: k absent from D iff n_k=0; k present implies n_k=1 and its stored payload and effect ID match that unique effect. It holds initially. An absent-key transaction creates precisely one matching effect/record pair. Same-payload replay and conflict leave the pair unchanged. Sending, delaying, dropping, timeout, and checkpoint restoration do not change E,D. An atomic crash leaves either the pretransaction or posttransaction state, each satisfying the invariant. Serialized concurrent requests are covered by the same induction: after the first commits, all same-key requests replay or conflict. Thus n_k<=1 for every reachable state. Stable, unique task-to-key mapping then gives N_o<=1. This is a proof for the defined model, not a proof that an implementation realizes its atomicity.

reasoning_steps.title: 6. Separate safety, progress, and verified completion
reasoning_steps.argument: If at least one valid request for o is processed, either it creates the pair or finds the pair already present; hence N_o=1. With no processing, N_o=0 remains possible: safety does not imply progress. Even when N_o=1, losing all acknowledgments can leave the agent unable to verify completion. A matching delivered acknowledgment establishes commit in this model because it is generated only from a valid effect/record pair. Agent-declared success without such evidence must be scored separately from actual correctness. An acknowledgment from a broken service cannot inherit this soundness argument.

reasoning_steps.title: 7. Derive baseline and ambiguous-commit traces
reasoning_steps.argument: Write (N,d) for the task effect count and the number of its completed records; O denotes an ordinary service that appends on every processing and never writes D. T0, no fault: atomic processing followed by acknowledgment yields (1,1), with matching result/effect ID; O yields (1,0). T1, precommit request drop: timeout sees (0,0); skip leaves zero effects, while one delivered retry yields atomic (1,1) or O (1,0). T2, postcommit acknowledgment drop: timeout sees atomic (1,1) or O (1,0); skip preserves one effect; retry leaves atomic (1,1) by replay but produces O (2,0). T1 and T2 must expose identical agent histories at the timeout, while J and E distinguish their fault locations and effects. These counts follow directly from the transition rules and are expected outcomes, not executed observations.

reasoning_steps.title: 8. Derive the two separate-write crash counterexamples
reasoning_steps.argument: T3, effect-first naive implementation: check D absent, durably append effect, crash before recording completion. State is (1,0). On restart a retry sees no record, appends a second effect, then writes D, giving (2,1). T4, record-first naive implementation: durably write a completed success record, crash before appending the effect. State is (0,1). A retry interprets the record as complete and returns success without creating the effect, preserving (0,1). Both violate the invariant, and T4 also invalidates acknowledgment soundness. These counterexamples concern records treated as completed, not a richer pending/resolved protocol. A pending record with reconciliation requires its own state machine and proof; the traces do not show that all separately implemented protocols are impossible.

reasoning_steps.title: 9. Distinguish delayed requests from dropped requests
reasoning_steps.argument: T5: delay the original request, let its timeout cause a retry, process the retry, then release the original. O has N=1 after the retry but N=2 after the late original. The atomic service remains at (1,1), because the late original replays. Therefore an evaluator that checks only at the agent's terminal message can incorrectly accept O. For this finite suite, stop new sends and drain all scheduled requests before final assessment, or require an audited fence that prevents outstanding requests from ever committing. Report deadline correctness separately from post-drain correctness. If delays are unbounded and there is no such fence, a finite observation of N=1 alone does not certify that no later duplicate will occur.

reasoning_steps.title: 10. Add boundary tests for identity, retention, payloads, and concurrency
reasoning_steps.argument: T6: commit under k, lose acknowledgment, restore/replan with new key k'; atomic processing under k' produces a second effect for the same o. T7: commit, delete D[k] while retaining E, then deliver an old retry; a second effect appears. T8: retry k with changed payload; the specified service returns conflict and preserves the existing effect. T9: give two intended operations the same key and identical payload; replay leaves the second operation missing despite both calls receiving success, demonstrating why protocol key uniqueness is a task-level requirement. T10: concurrently deliver two same-key attempts; serialized atomic handling creates one effect. As a negative control, a naive check-then-write service can let both attempts observe absence, append twice, and overwrite the same record. These tests isolate violations of the lemma's premises rather than refuting the lemma.

reasoning_steps.title: 11. Turn traces into a causal recovery evaluation

reasoning_steps.title: Scope and treatment of prior evidence
reasoning_steps.argument: The supplied extract of artifact 984e8fd3-f76b-46fb-b868-378c2f103425 proposes indistinguishable pre-commit and post-commit-loss histories and identifies missing harness and atomicity audits. I adopt that setup as a design to test, not as verified implementation evidence. Its original is unavailable here, several fields are truncated, and another finding is omitted. The argument below independently specifies and analyzes a narrower single-operation model; it neither certifies the earlier artifact nor resolves its omitted obligations. The transfer is appropriate only for irreversible, non-idempotent operations with an authoritative effect ledger, not arbitrary open-ended agent tasks.

reasoning_steps.title: Define actual effects, records, observations, and success
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix one authorized logical operation tau with key k and exact payload p. Durable actual-effect state E is a multiset of entries (tau,k,p,r), where r is an effect receipt; N is the number of entries for tau across all keys. Durable deduplication state D maps keys to completed (payload,receipt) pairs. The agent has local checkpoint C, including its intended operation, key, payload, and status, plus visible transcript V. Network state Q contains pending request and response envelopes. Volatile service state W contains in-progress work. Evaluator-only state J records fault events, commit order, and snapshots of E,D,Q; the agent cannot read J or inspect E,D directly. The experiment's physical correctness predicate is N=1 with the intended payload. Agent-reported completion and receipt availability are separately scored. The base case is E empty and D empty.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify network, crash, and observation semantics
reasoning_steps.argument: Sending adds an envelope to Q. Dropping a request permanently removes it without delivery or effect; delaying it leaves it in Q, eligible for later delivery. Delivering a request invokes the service. A response is enqueued only after the relevant service transition; response loss does not undo a commit. Timeout changes C and V but not E,D,Q. An agent crash restores its checkpoint; a service crash discards W while retaining durable E,D. Neither crash implicitly cancels pending network requests. Fault tests explicitly control queue persistence and delivery order. To construct the paired ambiguous histories, expose the same request bytes, local checkpoint, timeout text, elapsed time, and visible metadata up to recovery. Their evaluator logs may differ, but those logs must not leak through tools, memory, or orchestration. This equality is a harness requirement, not an observed property.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the atomic service contract
reasoning_steps.argument: For a delivered request (tau,k,p), service processing is serialized per key. If D[k] is absent, one durable atomic transition appends exactly one matching effect to E and installs D[k]=(p,r). If D[k]=(p,r) already exists, the service returns r without changing E or D. If the stored payload differs, it returns a conflict without changing either state. A crash overlapping the atomic transition leaves either its entire pre-state or entire post-state, never only one durable write. Records remain available throughout the retry horizon; no other actor creates effects for tau or mutates these records. For the theorem, all requests for tau use the same k,p, and distinct authorized operations do not share k. An effect means the business action inside this atomic boundary; a database record alone does not establish atomicity of a downstream physical shipment or unrelated external API call.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove safety and state the separate progress condition
reasoning_steps.argument: Initially N=0 and D[k] is absent. Maintain the invariant: either N=0 and D[k] is absent, or N=1 and D[k] records that effect with payload p. Send, delay, drop, timeout, checkpoint restoration, response delivery, and response loss do not modify E,D. A crash preserves an invariant-satisfying durable state. A first atomic commit changes the first invariant case to the second; every later same-key request is a no-op on E,D. Payload conflicts are also no-ops. Induction over any finite transition sequence therefore gives N<=1. Concurrent arrivals do not invalidate the induction because their commit transitions are serialized per key. If at least one request performs the first successful commit, N becomes 1 and remains 1. Without such a commit, N=0 is possible indefinitely. Thus safety does not imply delivery, timely completion, or that the agent learns success; receiving a matching response requires an additional communication condition.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the control and ambiguous-commit traces
reasoning_steps.argument: Notation: state pairs below are (N, presence of D[k]); an ordinary append service never uses D. T0, no-fault control: deliver one request and its response; ordinary and atomic services both end with N=1. T1, pre-commit request loss: send, permanently drop, timeout, then deliver a retry. Ordinary service goes 0 to 1; atomic service goes (0,absent) to (1,present). T2, post-commit response loss: deliver the first request, commit, drop its response, timeout, then deliver a retry. Ordinary service goes 0 to 1 to 2; atomic service goes (0,absent) to (1,present) to (1,present). T1 and T2 must have identical agent-visible prefixes through the recovery decision but different evaluator-visible effect counts. Skipping recovery leaves N=0 in T1 and N=1 in T2. A checkpoint that merely restores the same local intent cannot distinguish those prefixes. These counts follow from the transition definitions, not an executed harness.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct crash counterexamples for naive split writes
reasoning_steps.argument: T3, effect-first mutant: on an absent key, durably append the effect, then separately write D. Crash between writes, lose the response, and recover with (N=1,D absent). A retry sees absence, appends another effect, and eventually writes D; the final count is N=2. T4, record-first mutant: durably write a record treated as completed, then separately append the effect. Crash between writes and recover with (N=0,D present). A retry replays the stored receipt without appending; the count remains N=0 even if the agent receives a success-shaped response. In the atomic service, a crash at that logical boundary recovers only (0,absent) or (1,present), and a delivered retry yields N=1 in either case. These traces refute the two stated mutants, not every non-atomic implementation: a durable intent protocol with reconciliation, for example, requires its own state machine and proof.

reasoning_steps.title: Test delayed arrivals, concurrency, and assumption violations
reasoning_steps.argument: T5, delayed original: retain the first request in Q, timeout, deliver and commit the retry, then deliver the original. Ordinary service ends with N=2; atomic same-key service ends with N=1. This distinguishes request loss from delay and prevents an early evaluator snapshot from hiding a late duplicate. T6, concurrent duplicates: deliver two equal-key requests concurrently; the atomic contract admits only one first commit and hence N=1. An implementation allowing both workers to observe absence and append fails this test. T7, payload mismatch: after committing (k,p), send (k,p') with p' unequal to p; require a conflict and unchanged E,D. T8, unstable identity: after an ambiguous first commit, retry the same logical operation with a new key k'; per-key deduplication permits N=2. T9, record expiry: commit, remove D[k], and retry the original request; N can become 2. T8 and T9 deliberately leave the theorem's assumptions and test whether a deployment preserves them. They do not contradict the conditional invariant.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the harness audit and outcome oracle
reasoning_steps.argument: Each trace must retain evaluator-only before/after E,D snapshots, request identity and payload, send/delivery/drop order, durable-write boundaries, crash/restart points, restored checkpoint, and the complete agent-visible prefix. Check both requested fault placement and resulting state; a fault label alone is insufficient. Independently compare the two ambiguous prefixes field by field, including elapsed-time and orchestration channels; a byte comparison alone cannot establish that unrecorded channels are absent. Audit E against the controlled service's effect sink, rather than deriving effects from D or the agent's report, since T3 and T4 specifically separate those quantities. Before calling a trial settled, deliver all intentionally delayed envelopes or establish an enforced cancellation boundary. At a finite budget cutoff with live requests, report observed count and pending exposure separately; do not claim final duplicate-free success. This oracle is restricted to a controlled effect sink, not a solution to independent judging of open-ended tasks.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the discriminating architectural comparison
reasoning_steps.argument: First run scripted identical request sequences against ordinary append, atomic deduplication, and the two split-write mutants under T0–T9. This isolates service semantics from model behavior; the mutants are negative controls. Then substitute real agent policies, preserving model/prompt versions and paired task/environment snapshots, and measure whether identity and payload survive retries, restoration, replanning, and concurrent workers. Randomize mechanism assignment within task/fault blocks and repeat stochastic trials with documented seeds; keep budget caps equal and report realized resource use separately. Primary outcomes are audited intended-effect success, missing/duplicate/wrong effects, and false completion. Secondary outcomes include pending operations at cutoff, retry count, latency, and total trial cost per verified success, counting failed-trial cost in the numerator and reporting no-success denominators explicitly. Report paired uncertainty with task-level clustering rather than treating repeated runs on one task as independent task evidence. Keep diagnostic fault strata separate from deployment-weighted estimates until fault frequencies are measured. A gain only on T2 does not establish workflow-wide or held-out reliability.

strategy_snapshot.title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
Test architectural mechanisms for dependable agent outcomes

problem:
Autonomous AI agents are increasingly expected to complete complex tasks involving planning, reasoning, external tools, persistent state, and interaction with changing environments. Demonstrations and benchmark results show that agents can perform many such tasks, but provide limited evidence that they remain dependable across repeated executions, unfamiliar conditions, long-running workflows, and settings where mistakes have significant consequences. This project asks how autonomous and semi-autonomous agents can be evaluated and engineered to deliver reliable, correct, recoverable, and reproducible results across extended, multi-step tasks.

Agent reliability is a system-level property. Probabilistic decisions, dynamically constructed plans, incomplete observations, tool interfaces, memory, orchestration, and external state all affect whether the intended outcome is actually achieved. Small errors can propagate through later actions and yield plausible but incorrect results. An agent may claim completion without satisfying the task, recover from one failure while introducing another, or behave differently across otherwise comparable runs. Reliability therefore cannot be inferred from fluent explanations, a single successful trajectory, agreement among similar models, or benchmark scores alone.

Investigate three connected questions. First, how should reliability be defined and measured so evaluation reflects actual correctness, robustness, consistency, recoverability, tool-use quality, and cost rather than superficial completion? Second, what are the principal sources of failure, how do errors propagate through multi-step execution, and which signals and interventions can detect, contain, or recover from failures without creating additional risks? Third, which engineering mechanisms demonstrably improve outcomes, and how can their effects be established through controlled experiments rather than architectural intuition or anecdotal success? The strategies approach these questions from complementary measurement, failure-analysis, and intervention perspectives; none presumes a preferred architecture.

Use available research literature, software-reliability principles, empirical evaluation methods, and documented agent-system designs. Examine the relationship between model capability and end-to-end system reliability, including tool interfaces, state management, verification, orchestration, uncertainty handling, changing environments, recovery, and execution budgets. Assess benchmark sensitivity to task selection, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Consider stochastic behavior, repeated trials, long dependency chains, held-out tasks, fault injection, independent correctness judgments, and uncertainty in estimated success rates. Where comparisons are proposed, make assumptions and controls explicit, including model and prompt versions, task difficulty, environment, tool access, compute, latency, and monetary budgets.

Evaluate competing approaches on the strength and limits of their evidence. Distinguish measured results from formal or theoretical arguments, proposed mechanisms, and unsupported claims; do not present planned experiments as completed or infer causal benefit from correlation. Account for correlated errors among agents or critics that share models and training data, and for the difficulty of constructing an independent oracle for open-ended tasks. Analyze tradeoffs among reliability, flexibility, recovery overhead, latency, and computational expense, including cases where a safeguard shifts rather than removes risk.

The intended outcome is an evidence-grounded account of what reliability claims current evaluations can support, a practical and reproducible evaluation framework, a causal taxonomy of important failure and recovery modes, and architectural principles whose limits are explicit. Identify unresolved questions and specify discriminating experiments needed to validate competing claims. The project is open-ended: conclusions should remain proportional to the quality, independence, and generality of available evidence.

reasoning_steps.title: Define a protocol-specific reliability target
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix a task distribution D, an execution budget, model/prompt/tool versions, an r-run execution protocol, and a correctness rubric. For a task drawn from D, let Y_j be actual binary correctness of run j, A_j the routine oracle's acceptance, and R_j the reference judge's acceptance. Define p = E[(1/r) sum_j Y_j], a random-run success rate for this protocol, and z = E[(1/r) sum_j R_j]. This target is not probability that all r runs succeed, pass-at-r, or probability of an indefinitely safe workflow.

reasoning_steps.title: Replace perfect reference correctness with explicit error allowances
reasoning_steps.argument: For a uniformly selected run within the task batch, suppose P(R=1,Y=0) <= epsilon_plus and P(R=0,Y=1) <= epsilon_minus, with both allowances in [0,1]. These are unconditional error masses on the target distribution, not conditional error rates given acceptance or failure. They permit arbitrary dependence between A, R, and Y. If false rejection is unconstrained, use epsilon_minus=1. No supplied data establish either allowance.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive sharp population identification bounds
reasoning_steps.argument: Write f_plus=P(R=1,Y=0) and f_minus=P(R=0,Y=1). Partitioning the four possible (R,Y) outcomes gives p=z-f_plus+f_minus. Consequently max(0,z-epsilon_plus) <= p <= min(1,z+epsilon_minus). The endpoints are attainable without further restrictions: for the lower endpoint, label min(epsilon_plus,z) of the R=1 mass incorrect and all R=0 mass incorrect; for the upper endpoint, label all R=1 mass correct and min(epsilon_minus,1-z) of the R=0 mass correct. These assignments also satisfy the opposite error allowance, because its error mass is zero. Thus no uniformly narrower population interval follows from z and these allowances alone, even if the joint distribution of A and R is known.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct estimators using independent task units, not independent runs
reasoning_steps.argument: On N evaluation tasks let X_i=(1/r) sum_j A_ij and q_hat=(1/N) sum_i X_i. On m audit tasks where both judges score every run, let W_k=(1/r) sum_j(R_kj-A_kj) and w_hat=(1/m) sum_k W_k. Assume the evaluation clusters are independent and identically sampled, as are the audit clusters, and both follow the same target distribution and execution protocol. Dependence within a task is unrestricted, including dependence across its runs and judges. Then X_i lies in [0,1], W_k lies in [-1,1], and E[q_hat+w_hat]=E[A]+E[R-A]=z. Independence between the evaluation and audit panels is not needed for the union-bound argument below, though each panel must satisfy its own cluster assumptions.

reasoning_steps.title: Obtain a finite-sample confidence interval
reasoning_steps.argument: For 0<alpha<1 and positive integers N,m,r, put h_N=sqrt(log(4/alpha)/(2N)), h_m=sqrt(2 log(4/alpha)/m), eta=h_N+h_m, and c=clip(q_hat+w_hat,0,1). The bounded-variable concentration inequality gives P(|q_hat-E[A]|>h_N)<=alpha/2 and P(|w_hat-E[R-A]|>h_m)<=alpha/2. Specifically, for independent variables in an interval of length b, the centered sample mean has moment-generating function at most exp(t^2 b^2/(8n)); applying exponential Markov bounds to both tails and optimizing t yields 2 exp(-2n h^2/b^2). Here b=1 and b=2 respectively. A union bound therefore gives |q_hat+w_hat-z|<=eta with probability at least 1-alpha. Projection onto [0,1] cannot increase distance to z. Combining this event with the preceding identification bounds yields L=max(0,c-eta-epsilon_plus) and U=min(1,c+eta+epsilon_minus), with P(L<=p<=U)>=1-alpha.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate statistical uncertainty from unvalidated reference assumptions
reasoning_steps.argument: The preceding coverage statement is conditional on the error allowances being valid; it does not validate them. If a separate calibration procedure supplies simultaneous valid allowances with probability at least 1-beta, the same construction covers with probability at least 1-alpha-beta by another union bound, provided calibration targets these same error masses and protocol. Independence from calibration is not required for that union bound. Unknown systematic reference error must not be replaced by zero, and agreement among similar judges does not supply beta or either allowance.

reasoning_steps.title: Show why agreement cannot identify correctness
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider observed outputs A=R=1 on every run. One possible world has Y=1 always; another has Y=0 always. The observable judge records are identical, but p is respectively 1 or 0. Mixtures realize every intermediate p. Without a justified false-certification allowance or other correctness information, reliability is therefore unidentified despite perfect agreement. With epsilon_plus=epsilon_minus=1, the derived interval correctly becomes [0,1]. This is a logical counterexample to agreement-based certification, not an observed agent result.

reasoning_steps.title: Provide an independently derived dependence control
reasoning_steps.argument: For a proposed coverage test, draw one task type T~Bernoulli(1/2) and set all five repeated outcomes A_j=R_j=Y_j=T. The target p is 1/2. If the five repeats are incorrectly treated as five independent Bernoulli trials, observing five successes gives the conventional one-sided exact-binomial lower limit (1/20)^(1/5) at alpha=1/20. This exceeds 1/2 because 1/20>1/32. Five successes occur with probability 1/2 under the actual clustered process, so that purported 95% lower bound excludes the true value with probability at least 1/2. Counting task clusters instead avoids this unsupported fivefold sample-size claim. This construction independently demonstrates the failure mode recorded in the pointer-only ledger, without claiming inspection of its original example.

reasoning_steps.argument: This is a sufficient measurement construction, not a claim that separate oracle estimation and discrepancy auditing are necessary. Directly estimating the reference acceptance rate on audited tasks, followed by the same error allowances, is also valid and may be tighter. The proposed discrepancy construction can exploit a larger routine-evaluation panel, but no universal precision advantage is established. The sharpness claim concerns population identification, not optimality of the conservative confidence interval. No engineering intervention, actual benchmark, or deployment generalization has been evaluated.

reasoning_steps.title: 1. Separate business effects, service records, agent state, and audit state
reasoning_steps.argument: Let o denote one intended operation, k its protocol key, and p its complete canonical payload. Define state S=(E,D,Q,A,V,J). E is the durable business-effect ledger: entries contain effect ID, key, payload, and an evaluator-only attribution to o. N_o counts actual effects attributable to o, including those created under a mistakenly regenerated key. D is the service's durable map k -> (payload, result, effect ID), not an independent correctness oracle. Q contains request and acknowledgment envelopes, each with a distinct attempt ID. A contains agent memory and its durable checkpoint, including intended k,p. V is the entire agent-accessible event history. J is evaluator-only scheduling and fault history. Initially E and D are empty for the operations tested. The benchmark uses a synthetic durable append as its business effect; treating a database row as evidence of a real shipment would require a separate oracle.

reasoning_steps.title: 2. Define transport, timeout, and crash semantics
reasoning_steps.argument: Sending creates a request envelope in Q but changes neither E nor D. A dropped envelope is permanently removed without delivery. A delayed envelope remains eligible for later delivery, including after a retry. An acknowledgment is a separate envelope and can independently be delivered, dropped, or delayed. Timeout appends a fixed timeout event to V; it does not cancel an outstanding request or imply noncommitment. A service crash preserves E and D and discards volatile work. A crash before an atomic commit leaves neither write; a crash after it leaves both. Agent restoration restores A from its checkpoint but changes neither E nor D. The scheduler must explicitly record the disposition of every outstanding envelope; a crash is not an implicit request drop.

reasoning_steps.title: 3. Specify the agent observation boundary and ambiguous pair
reasoning_steps.argument: For paired histories, use the same local intent, serialized outgoing request, checkpoint, logical timeout time, returned bytes, headers, error metadata, tool access, and visible resource counters. In H0, drop the initial request before processing; in H1, process it and drop its acknowledgment. Hide E,D,J and queue internals from the agent. At the recovery decision, the specified projection V,A is identical, while evaluator-visible N_o is respectively 0 and 1. This constructs indistinguishability inside the abstract interface; it does not establish that a real harness prevents timing, billing, memory, or tool-status leakage. Any such leakage must be audited rather than assumed away.

reasoning_steps.title: 4. Define the atomic deduplicating service
reasoning_steps.argument: Processing a request (k,p) is one serialized transaction. If k is absent, append exactly one effect e to E and set D[k]=(p,result(e),e) atomically and durably, then enqueue an acknowledgment. If k is present with the same complete payload, enqueue its saved result without changing E or D. If k is present with a different payload, return a conflict without an effect. Retries retain k,p; distinct intended operations have distinct keys. There is no record eviction during any request's possible arrival horizon. No other actor changes E or D. The effect must actually be within this atomic boundary: atomically recording an intention before calling a nontransactional external API does not satisfy the premise.

reasoning_steps.title: 5. Prove the safety invariant
reasoning_steps.argument: For every key k, let n_k be its effect count. The invariant is: k absent from D iff n_k=0; k present implies n_k=1 and its stored payload and effect ID match that unique effect. It holds initially. An absent-key transaction creates precisely one matching effect/record pair. Same-payload replay and conflict leave the pair unchanged. Sending, delaying, dropping, timeout, and checkpoint restoration do not change E,D. An atomic crash leaves either the pretransaction or posttransaction state, each satisfying the invariant. Serialized concurrent requests are covered by the same induction: after the first commits, all same-key requests replay or conflict. Thus n_k<=1 for every reachable state. Stable, unique task-to-key mapping then gives N_o<=1. This is a proof for the defined model, not a proof that an implementation realizes its atomicity.

reasoning_steps.title: 6. Separate safety, progress, and verified completion
reasoning_steps.argument: If at least one valid request for o is processed, either it creates the pair or finds the pair already present; hence N_o=1. With no processing, N_o=0 remains possible: safety does not imply progress. Even when N_o=1, losing all acknowledgments can leave the agent unable to verify completion. A matching delivered acknowledgment establishes commit in this model because it is generated only from a valid effect/record pair. Agent-declared success without such evidence must be scored separately from actual correctness. An acknowledgment from a broken service cannot inherit this soundness argument.

reasoning_steps.title: 7. Derive baseline and ambiguous-commit traces
reasoning_steps.argument: Write (N,d) for the task effect count and the number of its completed records; O denotes an ordinary service that appends on every processing and never writes D. T0, no fault: atomic processing followed by acknowledgment yields (1,1), with matching result/effect ID; O yields (1,0). T1, precommit request drop: timeout sees (0,0); skip leaves zero effects, while one delivered retry yields atomic (1,1) or O (1,0). T2, postcommit acknowledgment drop: timeout sees atomic (1,1) or O (1,0); skip preserves one effect; retry leaves atomic (1,1) by replay but produces O (2,0). T1 and T2 must expose identical agent histories at the timeout, while J and E distinguish their fault locations and effects. reasoning_steps.title: 8. Derive the two separate-write crash counterexamples

A retry interprets the record as complete and returns success without creating the effect, preserving (0,1). Both violate the invariant, and T4 also invalidates acknowledgment soundness. prior_session_findings.strategy_title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability

reasoning_steps.title: Define the operation, objective, and observation boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider an agent instructed to cause exactly one irreversible external effect, such as appending one shipment order. Each accepted ordinary request creates one effect; there is no built-in deduplication. Let N be the external effect count for this task. Correctness is N=1, not merely receiving a plausible response. The agent records the same local intent before sending the request. At a timeout, its accessible checkpoint, messages, and observations do not reveal whether that request committed. Assume the only terminal recovery choices are skip or one retry; the retry, if chosen, commits exactly one additional effect. This intentionally restricted model isolates ambiguous-commit recovery rather than arbitrary tool or model errors.

review.rationale: The operation, success predicate N=1, observation boundary, and restricted terminal actions define a coherent model. They are accepted as premises only because the claim is explicitly conditional on them.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct two indistinguishable fault histories
reasoning_steps.argument: In history H0, the initial request is lost before commitment, leaving N=0. In history H1, the request commits, leaving N=1, but its acknowledgment is lost. Both histories end at the same timeout with the same local intent record and no acknowledgment. By assumption, no authoritative status lookup or other distinguishing observation is available before the decision. Therefore a policy using only that local information must use the same retry probability q in both histories. Random internal reasoning or replanning cannot distinguish two histories when its inputs and randomization distribution are identical.

review.rationale: Given identical accessible histories and identical policy-randomization distributions, a local-information policy must assign the same probability to retrying. H0 and H1 differ only in evaluator-visible external effect count.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the sharp worst-case error bound
reasoning_steps.argument: In H0, skipping leaves N=0 and retrying yields N=1, so the error probability is e0=1-q. In H1, skipping preserves N=1 and retrying yields N=2, so e1=q. Consequently e0+e1=1 and max(e0,e1)>=1/2. Equality is attained by q=1/2, making the bound sharp within this model. The deterministic edge cases q=0 and q=1 each fail with probability one in one history. This is a worst-case bound over two possible histories, not an assertion that either history occurs equally often in deployment.

review.rationale: Under the stipulated successful retry, H0 fails exactly when the policy skips, whereas H1 fails exactly when it retries. Thus e0=1-q, e1=q, their sum is one, and their maximum is at least one half; q=1/2 attains equality.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate worst-case reliability from deployment-average reliability
reasoning_steps.argument: If H1 has known conditional probability p among ambiguous timeouts, expected error is (1-p)(1-q)+pq. This affine function is minimized at q=1 when p<1/2, at q=0 when p>1/2, and by any q when p=1/2. The minimum is min(p,1-p). Thus an excellent average result can coexist with certain failure in the rarer history. The expression applies only within the ambiguous-timeout population and with equal weighting of missing and duplicate effects; it is not an overall task failure rate or an appropriate loss function when duplicate effects are more harmful.

review.rationale: Weighting the two conditional errors by 1-p and p gives 1-p+(2p-1)q. Its slope yields the stated optimal endpoint policies and minimum min(p,1-p). The equal-loss and ambiguous-timeout conditioning restrictions are explicitly preserved.
